title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Wind Turbines | MPI, US
description: Magnetic particle inspection of wind tower welds, flanges, bolts, shafts and nacelle frames at US fabrication plants and turbine sites. Request an MT quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Wind Turbines: MT of Tower Welds, Bolts, Shafts and Frames
html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection (MT, MPI or mag particle testing) on the steel and iron parts of onshore wind turbines in the United States: tower flange and seam welds, tower bolts and studs, main shafts, nacelle frames and gearbox housings. Technicians are mobilized to a fabrication plant, a yard or a turbine site, depending on the part and the scope. Blades are composite and outside our work. Request an MT inspection quote with the component list and drawings.

Why MT suits wind turbine steel

Wind turbine structures fail by fatigue. Tiny cracks start where stress is highest, which is nearly always at a surface: the toe of a flange weld, a thread root, the fillet under a bolt head, the edge of a door cutout. MT finds those cracks on ferromagnetic steel faster than any other method. Magnetizing the part makes a crack leak magnetic flux, and iron particles gather over it to form a sharp line a technician can read at once. It handles rough, painted-over-light and as-welded surfaces better than penetrant testing, and it needs no dwell time.

It also has limits. MT sees only surface and shallow subsurface flaws and reads nothing about wall thickness. It cannot be used on nonmagnetic parts. For internal weld flaws in thick tower sections we add ultrasonic testing for wind turbines, and for nonmagnetic hardware liquid penetrant testing for wind turbines. The overview of the method sits on our magnetic particle testing page.

Tower welds and flange connections

Tower cans are joined by circumferential welds, and heavy flanges are welded to the ends. During fabrication the specification, typically AWS D1.1 or the manufacturer's own document, calls for visual and magnetic particle examination of selected welds in addition to ultrasonic testing. MT is used on the weld face and toe to confirm no surface cracks or undercut-related flaws after welding and grinding, and on repair excavations before and after refilling. At door frames, platform brackets and cable support attachments the weld is small, the geometry is tight and cracks are likely to start at the weld toe, so these locations are examined by MT even when the long seams are not. The job page on magnetic particle inspection of structural steel describes the technique for weldments of this type.

For in-service towers, owners examine flange welds and door frames after a fault or a suspected overload. This work is done from inside the tower where possible, so we look for lighting, power and safe access in the quote request.

Bolts, studs and threaded connections

High-strength bolts and studs in tower flanges and anchor connections carry heavy cyclic tension. Cracks form in the first engaged thread and at the head-to-shank fillet. For bolts that have been removed, MT with a coil or a central conductor induces a longitudinal or circular field so cracks across the thread root appear as lines. Fluorescent wet particles under black light give the sensitivity this work needs and make cracks stand out against the thread form. High-strength bolts can be sensitive to arc burns and to hydrogen effects, so we do not use prods on them and the examiner demagnetizes after the examination when the specification asks.

Bolts left in place are screened by ultrasonic methods rather than MT, which would need access to every thread. Where a few bolts are removed after a failure, MT on those samples helps the owner decide if the problem is isolated.

Main shafts, bearing housings and nacelle frames

Main shafts are forged and machined carbon or alloy steel. MT is used at fillets, keyways and bearing seat transitions where fatigue cracks start, normally with the shaft exposed during a bearing or gearbox replacement. Nacelle frames and bedplates may be welded plate or ductile iron castings, both magnetic, and both suitable for MT at weld toes, casting parting lines and machined mounting pads. Gearbox and bearing housings are examined in the same way after repair or when the manufacturer calls for it. Where a manufacturer's requirements apply to a shaft or housing, those documents control over any general practice.

Technique: yoke, field direction and cold weather

Plant and yard work normally uses a hand-held AC yoke with lifting power checked on the test block, which follows ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E709 practice. We use dry powder for rough as-welded surfaces and wet particles, visible or fluorescent, where greater sensitivity is needed. Each area is examined in two directions about ninety degrees apart, so a crack parallel to one field direction is still caught by the other. For bolts and shafts, a coil or contact heads may be used, with the technique set in the procedure.

Cold weather matters on wind sites. Wet suspension carriers thicken when it gets cold and particles migrate slowly, so for winter work we select a carrier rated for the temperature or switch to dry powder, and we keep batteries and instruments warm. In towers the light is poor, so we measure white light or black light intensity at the examination surface instead of assuming it. Our explainer on Section V Article 7 details the requirements, and the complete MT guide covers the underlying physics.

Production runs, repairs and planning

In a tower fabrication plant, MT is a production step rather than a one-off. Welds are examined after grinding and before blasting and coating, and a repair loop is common: a crack is found, ground out, the excavation is examined to confirm it is clear, the weld is refilled and the repaired area is examined again. We build that loop into the scope and report each pass separately, so the record shows the original indication, the excavation and the final result. Because coating follows, the fabricator tells us when each can is ready and whether the examination must happen before a coating schedule closes.

Planning for a field job is different. Turbine sites are remote, and a crew mobilized for a single bolt or housing check carries the same equipment as for a larger job. Sending the part list and a photo of the access in advance helps us bring the right yoke, coil, particles and lighting. Parts that have been coated in grease or oil need cleaning before MT, and fluorescent work inside a bright nacelle may need screening to get a dark enough area. The site arranges hoists, lifts and rope teams under its own safety plan, and our technicians follow site orientation and any badging or lockout rules in force at the wind farm.

Where a surface has been shot-peened or has a heavy galvanized layer, tell us in advance. A thin, tightly bonded coating can be examined through if the procedure has shown that indications still appear, but a thick or flaking layer must be removed along the examination path. Demagnetization is carried out when residual magnetism could affect later welding, machining or bearing assembly.

Codes and acceptance

AWS D1.1 governs structural steel welding for many towers; the turbine manufacturer adds its own requirements. Acceptance criteria, including the allowed length and number of indications, come from those documents and not from Atlantis. The report states the specification and revision. If a tower design falls under ASME rules instead, the corresponding construction code controls. Where the documents leave a gap, we ask the owner or fabricator for written direction before we examine.

Who performs the work

MT is performed by Level II technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with procedures approved and reports reviewed by an ASNT Level III. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. We do not set repair or retirement decisions; we report indications for the owner, manufacturer or engineer.

What the report contains

  • Project, turbine or tower identification and the components examined
  • Procedure number and revision, and the specification used for acceptance
  • Equipment: yoke or coil, particles, carrier, lifting power and light measurements
  • Surface condition and temperature
  • Technician name and qualification level
  • Each indication with location, orientation, length and accept or reject
  • Sketches, photographs and any limits on coverage

What to send for a quote

  • Drawings, weld maps and the specification with acceptance criteria
  • Part list with quantities: tower sections, bolts, shafts, frames
  • Material grade and surface condition, including coatings
  • Location: shop, yard or turbine, and the site address
  • Access method, power supply, lighting and fall protection plan
  • Schedule window and site orientation or badging requirements

What we do not do

We do not inspect blades or other composite parts. We do not perform radiography in the United States, because it is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 and Agreement State rules. We do not offer specialist techniques on this page. We do not decide how long a part can keep running or when it must be replaced.

Where we work in the US for wind energy

  • Omaha: Plains wind projects and the fabricators that supply them.
  • Wichita: Kansas wind farms and steel fabricators.
  • Oklahoma City: Oklahoma wind projects with long tower haul distances.
  • Denver: Rocky Mountain wind and fabrication.
  • Midland: West Texas wind farms.
  • Tulsa: weldments and fabricators in northeast Oklahoma.
  • Minneapolis: upper Midwest cold-weather wind work.
  • Albuquerque: New Mexico wind and dry, high-altitude conditions.

Training your own MT technicians

Wind fabricators and owner-operators who want in-house MT can start with MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and practice on the magnetic particle simulator. The manufacturing NDT training page suits fabrication shops. Since the employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A, we can help with a written practice and with procedure development. If you are weighing penetrant against magnetic particle, see our MT versus PT comparison.

faq.q: Which wind turbine parts can be inspected by magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Any ferromagnetic part: tower welds and flanges, bolts and studs, main shafts, nacelle frames, and steel or ductile iron housings. Aluminum, stainless steel and composite parts cannot be magnetized, so those need penetrant testing or another approach.

faq.q: Can MT be used on bolts that are still installed in the tower?
faq.a: Rarely. MT of threads needs access to the whole bolt, so we use it on bolts that have been removed. Installed bolts are screened by ultrasonic testing, and a sample removed afterward can be examined by MT.

faq.q: Who decides whether an MT indication in a tower weld is rejectable?
faq.a: The specification named in the report decides, usually AWS D1.1 or the turbine manufacturer's document. Atlantis reports indications against those criteria; repair decisions belong to the owner, manufacturer or engineer.

faq.q: Does cold weather stop magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Not necessarily. We use dry powder or a carrier rated for low temperature, keep equipment warm and measure light levels. If conditions fall outside what the procedure allows, the work waits until they are acceptable.

faq.q: Why MT instead of PT on tower welds?
faq.a: MT is faster, tolerates rough as-welded surfaces and needs no dwell time. PT is the choice for nonmagnetic metal or where a yoke cannot reach. We recommend MT first on tower steel.

faq.q: Do you use prods on high-strength bolts?
faq.a: No. Prods can leave arc burns, which damage high-strength fasteners. For bolts we use a coil or conductor, and we demagnetize after the examination when the specification requires it.

faq.q: What do you need to quote MT at a fabrication plant?
faq.a: Drawings or weld maps, the specification with acceptance criteria, part list and quantities, material and surface condition, location and access, schedule window, and the site address and any orientation requirements.

faq.q: Do you work on turbines at the wind farm as well as in the shop?
faq.a: Yes, for steel and iron parts, as the owner arranges safe access. The site provides cranes, lifts or rope access and its rescue plan. Our technicians are mobilized for the agreed scope.
No. Blades are composite structures and need different inspection methods that Atlantis does not offer. We examine only the steel and iron parts of the tower, nacelle and drive train.
